without_skill.expectation: Names custom DKIM signing with d= on petrel.dev (or a subdomain of it) as the first technical fix
Says the open-rate drop alone is not evidence of spam-folder placement, citing mail-privacy features or image blocking
Asks for or recommends Gmail Postmaster Tools spam-rate data and marks complaints unverified until it exists
Says Gmail 4.7.x or 5.7.x authentication replies, if present in the bounce log, are sender-side and must not be suppressed
Recommends checking the raw bounce or deferral replies (for example 4.7.32 or other 4.7.x/5.7.x codes) rather than platform hard/soft totals
Gives a fix plan where each row has an owner, a date and a done-when check
Applies a re-confirmation issue for a list silent this long (or names the programme's silent-list rule as the deciding fact), sent through the ramp with non-responders suppressed
States that a list-verification or cleaning service cannot reliably detect spam traps or prove readers still want the mail
Describes growing cohorts over several sends (roughly doubling, or over weeks) rather than one send
Labels the 2% bounce hold level as a house rule, not a provider rule
Sends the launch issue on Tuesday to the warm cohorts only and the rest over the following sending days
Asks whether click history exists to order cohorts, or says to fall back to signup date when it does not
Recommends reading each send's raw bounce replies before the next cohort
Gives a test order: GET the URL, confirm the seed is still subscribed, then POST, then confirm it is unsubscribed
Warns that the confirmation page must not auto-submit with JavaScript because some scanners execute it
Says the unsubscribe endpoint must not return a redirect to the POST
Says not to silently re-subscribe the readers removed by scanners, and to tell them how to resubscribe or restore only those who ask
States that the pct tag was removed by RFC 9989 (DMARCbis) because receivers applied partial values inconsistently
Names t=y test mode as the replacement for pct
Recommends rehearsing each enforcement level with t=y together with pct=0 so old and new receivers both apply one level lower
Recommends enforcing on the newsletter subdomain before the organizational domain
Notes that some receivers may still follow the old RFC 7489 behaviour during the transition
Describes t=y as an on/off test flag rather than a percentage ramp
Gives the order: monitor, inventory, subdomain enforcement, organizational domain enforcement
Recommends a warm-up for the new sending domain or subdomain
States that at a Gmail spam rate above 0.3% the sender is ineligible for Google mitigation until 7 consecutive days below it
Recommends stopping or slowing sends to the complaining segment before other fixes
Says to pause and escalate a receiver only if it still blocks two sends after the authentication fix is verified
Recommends Spamhaus's own lookup page rather than DNS queries through public resolvers, or warns that public-resolver lookups return misleading codes
Declines to give tricks for escaping Promotions, noting they risk complaints
Suggests the only sanctioned lever is asking readers to move the message or reply
Says requesting delisting before fixing the cause leads to being listed again
Names Microsoft Defender's Bulk Complaint Level and its default threshold of 7 moving bulk mail to Junk
Mentions that the Strict preset uses threshold 5 and quarantines, which fits regulated enterprises such as banks
Notes that the Standard preset uses threshold 6
Mentions that company admins can lower the bulk threshold
Advises against switching platforms as the fix, noting a switch resets signals and needs a warm-up
Recommends publishing allow-listing instructions for readers' IT teams naming the sending domain and DKIM d= rather than IPs
Mentions that Google Workspace corporate recipients fall outside Gmail's sender rules and follow their admins' policies
Notes that gateway link scanning can inflate clicks and recommends filtering them
Gives a monitoring or evidence step with an owner rather than a vague recommendation
